div.div: The same 3 % jump can be noise in 100 devices but is a fleet change in 10 000: the share's standard error shrinks with sqrt(n), so the trend test weights each day by n (illustrative counts)

Share of devices that emitted a rare disconnect reason, one day [A2]
dot = share; bar = +/- 1 standard error, SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
share of devices (%)

small family
100 [1*] active,
3 [2*] emit it
SE = 1.7 pp [3*]

large family
10 000 [4*] active
same share
SE = 0.17 pp [5*]
Halve n and SE grows by sqrt 2. Three unlucky households can make the small-family jump; the large-family bar is ten times tighter (sqrt of 100x the devices). Share 3 % = 3 / 100, my arithmetic.
1 one series per slice [B4]: daily share p_t and active count n_t per (family, feature, category) over 8 weeks [6*] (56 daily points)
2 not ordinary least squares [B4]: Var(p_t) = p(1-p)/n_t changes day to day (weekends, outages, new cohorts): heteroscedastic; OLS gives a noisy day the same say and a wrong slope SE
3 weighted least squares [B4]: weight w_t = n_t / (p_t(1-p_t)); minimise sum w_t (p_t - a - b t)^2. Use a pooled p when p_t is 0 or 1 (infinite weight)
4 test against a practical slope s [B4]: H0: b = s (not b = 0: with enough devices every slope is significant). One-sided p = 1 - Phi((b_hat - s) / se(b_hat))
5 p-value -> score [B4]: score = -10 [7] log10(p), capped at 100 [8*]; see the ladder below

6 filter direction, control false discoveries [B4]: drop good-direction changes; 10 000 series/day [9*] tested at p 0.01 give about 100 series/day [10*] by chance -> FDR control or rank and read the top
p -> score ladder (each 10 points = 10x smaller p) [B4]

p = 1e-5
score 50 [11]

p = 1e-10 (cap)
score 100 [11]
Family level [B4]: WLS slope test on the share. Catches fleet-wide regressions (a release that raises disconnects). Few reports (e.g. 1 [12*] per week), each high impact.
Device level [B3, B4]: isolation forest on device-day vectors. Catches one device or household behaving oddly. Many reports, each lower impact and often environmental.

Read it correctly [B4]: the score is a confidence that the slope exceeds s, not a severity; a significant trend can be a router-firmware rollout, a holiday or a reporting change. Correlated daily residuals make se(b) too small: check with a weekly dummy.

Legend — red = small population (noisy); green = large population (precise); blue = estimation steps; amber = the decision steps (threshold, score); purple = device-level detection. pp = percentage points.

Sources — every number is loaded from ../constants.json. [n] = public (real value, cited); [n*] = illustrative (an invented round number of realistic order of magnitude; never a measurement).
[1*] small_family_devices = 100 active devices — illustrative
[2*] rare_reason_devices = 3 devices — illustrative
[3*] rare_share_small_family_se = 1.7 percentage points — illustrative; my arithmetic: sqrt(0.03*0.97/100), from illustrative inputs
[4*] large_family_devices = 10 000 active devices — illustrative
[5*] rare_share_large_family_se = 0.17 percentage points — illustrative; my arithmetic: sqrt(0.03*0.97/10000), from illustrative inputs
[6*] trend_series_length = weeks 8, daily_points 56 weeks / days — illustrative
[7] phred_factor = 10 score points per decade of p — public; Ewing & Green, Genome Research 8:186-194, 1998: Q = -10 log10 P
[8*] score_cap = 100 score — illustrative; cap (p = 1e-10)
[9*] monitored_series = 10 000 series per day — illustrative
[10*] multiple_testing_false_alarms = 100 series per day — illustrative; my arithmetic: 10 000 x 0.01, illustrative inputs
[11] score_examples = p_0.1 10, p_0.01 20, p_1e-5 50, p_1e-10 100 score — public; my arithmetic from score = -10 log10(p)
[12*] family_reports_per_week = 1 reports — illustrative
